stops.name: Tübingen, the Stift: Schelling in the shared attic room
stops.date_confidence: attested, and inherited byte-identical from schelling.journey.json; the interlock lens rendered the latitude as 48.52 and the journey file's 48.521 is used instead
stops.campa: A hundred and thirty-eight years before Rogers is born, a boy of fifteen enters the Tübinger Stift and takes an attic cell with Hegel and Hölderlin. Friedrich Schelling will build a philosophy in which imagination is not ornament but the organ by which a people comes to know itself. An essay on make-believe later sets his name beside four others who each treated a child's imagination as a real faculty rather than a phase to be outgrown, and one of the four is a television host from western Pennsylvania. The line it draws runs straight through this attic room.
suggested_refs: The attic room of the Tübinger Stift shared by Schelling, Hegel and Hölderlin from October 1790

stops.name: Bad Blankenburg town hall, the kindergarten is named
stops.date_confidence: attested, and inherited byte-identical from froebel.journey.json; the interlock lens transcribed the longitude as 50.813, which would drop the pin into the Black Sea, and flagged its own error
stops.campa: In the town hall at Bad Blankenburg, Friedrich Froebel gives his institution for small children a name: kindergarten, a garden of children, where the gardener does not pull the shoot to make it grow. He has already designed the Gifts, sphere and cylinder and cube, and a Sunday paper written for the children themselves rather than about them. A hundred and twenty-eight years later a man in Pittsburgh will hold objects up to a camera and speak to one child at a time. Essay 174 makes the descent explicit.
suggested_refs: The Froebel Gifts, and the Bad Blankenburg town hall where the word kindergarten was adopted

stops.name: Hofwil, Itten carries the method into the Vorkurs
stops.date_confidence: attested, and inherited byte-identical from itten.journey.json
stops.campa: At the teacher-training college of Hofwil near Bern, Johannes Itten absorbs the kindergarten method of Friedrich Froebel in the reform tradition of Pestalozzi, where play is the instruction and the hand comes before the word. He will carry it into the Bauhaus Vorkurs at Weimar, and a century of design learns to begin with texture and contrast rather than with rules. The line runs Pestalozzi at Yverdon, Froebel at Blankenburg, Itten at Hofwil, and then a room in Pittsburgh with a front door and a model trolley in it.
suggested_refs: The Hofwil teacher-training college near Bern, and Itten's Vorkurs exercises at Weimar

stops.name: Paris, Steiner before Schuré's circle
stops.date_confidence: attested, and inherited byte-identical from steiner.journey.json; Blavatsky occupies the same pin on 1884-03-28 per blavatsky.journey.json
stops.campa: Rudolf Steiner lectures in Paris to the circle around Édouard Schuré, twenty-two years after Blavatsky stood on this same pin through the worst weeks of the Coulomb affair. Steiner is the fourth pedagogue essay 174 names beside Fred Rogers, and the schools that will carry his name teach, as Rogers does, that a child's imagination is a faculty and not a phase. The same essay names Wilhelm Reich's make-believe science of orgone in the same paragraph cluster. Then it turns to a man in a cardigan.
suggested_refs: Steiner's 1906 Paris lecture cycle before Édouard Schuré's circle

segments.name: Latrobe: Main Street, Weldon Street, the Piano

stops.name: 705 Main Street, Latrobe, the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and the street address; the coordinate is the Nominatim geocode of 705 Main Street, replacing the pool's 40.3167 / -79.3781, which sits about 250 m off
stops.campa: Fred McFeely Rogers is born on the principal commercial street of Latrobe, Pennsylvania, to James Hillis Rogers, president of the McFeely Brick Company, and to Nancy McFeely Rogers, whose family name the firm carries. He is their only biological child. The house stands among storefronts in a prosperous small town forty miles southeast of Pittsburgh, and the whole arc of his life will stay inside that forty miles, with four years in Toronto and two in New York cut out of the middle of it.
suggested_refs: 705 Main Street, Latrobe, and the McFeely Brick Company works

stops.name: 737 Weldon Street, the piano and the puppets
stops.date_confidence: the house and the childhood are attested; the year marks his beginning at the piano around age five and the month and day are placeholders; the coordinate is the Nominatim geocode, replacing the pool's 40.3145 / -79.3760, about 410 m south
stops.campa: The family lives in a large three-storey brick house on Weldon Street, and here the boy is asthmatic, overweight, and kept indoors. The neighbourhood calls him Fat Freddy. He is about five when he starts at the piano, and he plays alone for hours, inventing puppets to keep himself company in a house with no other children in it. There is a vacation place outside town with a pool where he learns to swim, and there are winter trips south to Florida. The piano is a refuge long before it is an instrument.
suggested_refs: The three-storey brick house at 737 Weldon Street, Latrobe
sources: OpenStreetMap Nominatim, 737 Weldon Street, Latrobe PA

stops.name: 737 Weldon Street, a sister is adopted
stops.date_confidence: attested only as happening when he was about eleven; the year is derived from that and the month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: When Fred is about eleven the Rogerses adopt a daughter, Elaine, and the solitary child of the brick house acquires a sibling. The standard telling calls him an only child. He is the only child born to them, which is a different sentence, and the difference sits oddly in a biography whose entire subject is what a household does to a small person. No witness set down what Elaine's arrival did to the boy at the piano, and the reachable record leaves the question open.
suggested_refs: Family photographs of Fred and Elaine Rogers at Weldon Street

stops.name: Latrobe High School, the graduation of 1946
stops.date_confidence: the graduation year is attested; the month is a placeholder and no consulted source gives the day, and the coordinate is approximate because the 1940s building may not correspond to the present campus
stops.campa: He leaves Latrobe High School as student council president, a member of the National Honor Society, and editor of the yearbook. That is the record of a boy who has stopped being the one at the window. He is eighteen and composing at the piano, and he means to study for the ministry. Latrobe will not have him as a resident again. He comes back for his father's funeral, then in a coffin to a private service in a chapel outside town, and at last as a name on a cast metal marker bolted up near the street where he was born.
suggested_refs: The 1946 Latrobe High School yearbook, edited by Rogers

segments.name: Hanover, Greensburg, Winter Park, Rockefeller Plaza

stops.name: Dartmouth College, Hanover, one year on the Green
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia attests one year at Dartmouth before the transfer to Rollins; the pool's range of 1946-1948 contradicted its own prose and is rejected, and the month is a placeholder for the start of the academic year
stops.campa: He enrolls at Dartmouth drawn to Romance languages and lasts a year. The college is wrong for him and he says so, and he leaves New Hampshire for a small music school in Florida. Fifty-six years later Dartmouth will ask him back to give the last commencement address of his life, and he will stand on this same Green and instruct a graduating class to sit for one unbroken minute in silence. He leaves this coordinate as a transfer student. He returns to it as the speaker.
suggested_refs: The Dartmouth Green, Hanover, New Hampshire

stops.name: Greensburg, the draft board and the legend
stops.date_confidence: the 1948 registration at Greensburg and the reclassification after an Armed Forces physical on 1950-10-12 are both attested; the month and day here are placeholders, the coordinate is Greensburg at large, and no source places the 1950 physical anywhere at all
stops.campa: At twenty he registers for the military draft at Greensburg and is classified 1-A. On the twelfth of October 1950 an Armed Forces physical finds him unqualified for service, and that is the end of it: he never serves. Half a century later the internet will insist he was a decorated sniper who wore long sleeves to cover his tattoos, and the correction most often circulated against it, that he was deferred as a divinity student, is also false. He will not enter the seminary for another five years.
suggested_refs: Rogers' 1948 Selective Service registration at Greensburg, Pennsylvania

stops.name: Rollins College, Winter Park, the transfer and Joanne Byrd
stops.date_confidence: the transfer to Rollins and the meeting with Sara Joanne Byrd there are attested; the month is a placeholder, and the coordinate is the Nominatim geocode of 1000 Holt Avenue, replacing the pool's 28.5978 / -81.3492, about 580 m north of campus
stops.campa: He transfers to Rollins College on the shore of Lake Virginia and reads music. Among the music students is Sara Joanne Byrd of Jacksonville, a pianist. The two will marry in four years and stay married for fifty-one, until a February morning in a Pittsburgh bedroom where she is the one sitting beside him. The boy who played alone in the brick house on Weldon Street is now in a conservatory, where playing alone is the assignment and the solitude has a name and a curriculum.
suggested_refs: Rollins College, 1000 Holt Avenue, Winter Park, and its music school of the late 1940s

stops.name: Rollins College, the Bachelor of Music, magna cum laude
stops.date_confidence: the 1951 degree in composition, magna cum laude, is attested; the month is a placeholder for commencement
stops.campa: He takes the degree in composition magna cum laude, and the college will name him its Outstanding Alumnus nineteen years later. He does not go on to the seminary. He goes to New York, into the new medium, and the seminary waits another four years for him. This music degree is the whole of his professional training: no journalism, no theatre, no schooling in education. Every song in the Neighborhood, and there will be hundreds of them, is written by a man trained here to write them.
suggested_refs: Rogers' 1951 Rollins College composition portfolio

stops.name: NBC, 30 Rockefeller Plaza, the floor director
stops.date_confidence: attested that he began at NBC in New York shortly after graduating in 1951; the month is a placeholder and no source gives a start date
stops.campa: Straight out of Rollins he joins NBC in New York as a floor director and assistant producer on musical variety: Your Hit Parade, The Kate Smith Hour. He is inside the industry at the moment it becomes national, standing under the lights with a headset, cueing singers into a camera. He learns in two years what a studio can be made to do. Then he leaves the largest broadcaster in the country for a station in Pittsburgh that has not yet put a single programme on the air.
suggested_refs: The NBC studios at 30 Rockefeller Plaza and the sets of Your Hit Parade

stops.name: Jacksonville, the marriage to Sara Joanne Byrd
stops.date_confidence: the year 1952 is attested and nothing else is; the pool's chronology lens gives the place as Jacksonville while its geography lens correctly records the ceremony site as undetermined, and that contradiction is left standing, the pin resting on the bride's hometown as a declared placeholder rather than a claim about where the wedding happened
stops.campa: He marries Sara Joanne Byrd, the pianist from the Rollins music school. She is from Jacksonville, Florida, and the marriage runs from this year unbroken to the February morning in 2003 when she is in the room. Fifty-one years. Of the wedding itself the record keeps nothing: not the church, not the town, not the month. It keeps only the span, and the span is the part that the rest of the life is built on. He is twenty-four years old and has been in television for one year.
suggested_refs: Any surviving 1952 marriage record for Fred Rogers and Sara Joanne Byrd, currently unlocated

segments.name: WQED: The Children's Corner, McFarland, the Ordination

stops.name: WQED, 4802 Fifth Avenue: a station with nothing on it yet
stops.date_confidence: the 1953 move to WQED is attested; the month is a placeholder, and the coordinate is the Nominatim geocode of 4802 Fifth Avenue, confirmed by the 2018 USPS release, replacing the pool's 40.4444 / -79.9508, which was about 600 m southwest and was repeated across seven entries
stops.campa: He goes home to Pennsylvania to help launch WQED, one of the first community-supported public television stations in the United States. It has a licence, a building on Fifth Avenue in Oakland, and almost no programming. For the next half century, with a Toronto interruption of four years, this address is where his working life happens. The studio inside it will eventually carry his name and appear on a first-day-of-issue postal release. He arrives having left network television on purpose.
suggested_refs: WQED, 4802 Fifth Avenue, Pittsburgh, in its first broadcast year

stops.name: WQED, The Children's Corner: the puppets born behind the set
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1954 for the start of the programme, with Rogers working the puppets and writing the music behind the set; the month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: With Josie Carey in front of the camera, Rogers works the puppets from behind the set, unseen, writing the music and speaking the voices. Daniel Striped Tiger is born here, and King Friday XIII, and X the Owl, years before any of them ride a trolley into a Neighborhood of Make-Believe. He is not the host and does not want to be. He is the hand inside the tiger and the composer at the piano offstage, learning that a child will say to a puppet what she will not say to an adult.
stops.quote: You were a child once, too.
stops.quote_source: Tom Junod, 'Can You Say...Hero?', Esquire, November 1998: the single sentence Rogers wrote to open a chapter addressed to ophthalmologists, after rejecting the draft written for him
suggested_refs: The original Daniel Striped Tiger and King Friday XIII puppets from The Children's Corner

stops.name: University of Pittsburgh, Margaret McFarland's classroom
stops.date_confidence: the study of child development under Margaret McFarland is attested but dated only to the 1950s and 1960s; this date is a declared placeholder inside that range, and the coordinate is carried from the pool without independent geocoding because no source names a building
stops.campa: While he works days at the station he studies child development under Margaret McFarland, and from her he takes the theory that will dictate everything: the pacing, the silences, the direct address, the refusal to hurry a sentence to its end. What Froebel worked out with wooden spheres in a Thuringian town hall arrives in this room as clinical psychology. The man taking notes is in his late twenties and already knows what he intends to do with it.
stops.quote: I feel that if we in public television can only make it clear that feelings are mentionable and manageable, we will have done a great service for mental health.
stops.quote_source: U.S. Senate Subcommittee on Communications testimony, 1 May 1969, transcript via Speakola and Current
suggested_refs: Margaret McFarland's papers on child development at the University of Pittsburgh

stops.name: Pittsburgh Theological Seminary, 616 North Highland Avenue
stops.date_confidence: the 1962 Bachelor of Divinity magna cum laude is attested, as is part-time study from the mid-1950s; the month is a placeholder, and the coordinate is the Nominatim geocode of 616 North Highland Avenue, replacing the pool's 40.4664 / -79.9280, which landed about 600 m west and off campus
stops.campa: Seven years of part-time study, taken on lunch hours and evenings around a full-time job in television, end in a Bachelor of Divinity magna cum laude. He now holds two degrees with the same honours, one in composition and one in divinity, and he has no pulpit and no congregation and no intention of acquiring either. What he has instead is a camera, a piano, and a tiger puppet. The presbytery is about to decide that these three things count as a parish.
suggested_refs: Pittsburgh Theological Seminary, 616 North Highland Avenue, and its 1962 graduating class

stops.name: Pittsburgh, the ordination with an unusual charge
stops.date_confidence: the ordaining body and the year 1963 are attested; the church or chapel of the ceremony is not given in any consulted source, so the coordinate is downtown Pittsburgh as a declared placeholder and the month and day are placeholders too
stops.campa: The Pittsburgh Presbytery of the United Presbyterian Church ordains him a minister and charges him, in place of a parish, to serve children and families through television. It is a strange commission and it is granted in plain terms. He will never preach from a pulpit. He will instead say, some fifty times a year for three decades, that a person is likeable exactly as he already is, which in the theology he was taught is the same sentence arrived at from the other side.
suggested_refs: The Pittsburgh Presbytery minutes of 1963 recording the charge to a television ministry

stops.name: CBC, 354 Jarvis Street, Toronto: Misterogers
stops.date_confidence: attested that the CBC contracted him in 1963 to develop and host Misterogers, which ran 1963-1967; the month is a placeholder, and the coordinate is the Nominatim geocode of the Jarvis Street studio, replacing the pool's 43.6629 / -79.3733, about 330 m off. The pool's note of a 1961 contradiction is withdrawn: no such date appears in the article
stops.campa: The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation brings him north to develop and host a fifteen-minute black-and-white children's programme, and puts him, for the first time in his life, in front of the lens. The title is Misterogers, one word. The furniture of the later American programme is already assembled here: the cardigan, the sneakers, the trolley, the door opened at the top of every episode. He is thirty-five and has spent nine years working from behind a set.
suggested_refs: Surviving black-and-white kinescopes of the CBC Misterogers, 1963-1967

stops.name: Toronto, Butternut Square and Ernie Coombs
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1964 for the work on Butternut Square with Ernie Coombs; the month and day are placeholders and the coordinate repeats the Jarvis Street studio pin
stops.campa: He works on the children's programme Butternut Square alongside a young American puppeteer named Ernie Coombs, who came up from Pittsburgh with him. When Rogers takes his own programme home in 1967, Coombs stays in Canada and becomes Mr. Dressup, and Canadian children get their own daily man with a costume trunk for the next thirty years. One migration south, one man left behind on purpose, and two countries end up with a version of the same room.
suggested_refs: Butternut Square, CBC, 1964, and the origins of Mr. Dressup

stops.name: WQED, the rights carried home
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1967 for the acquisition of the rights and the return to Pittsburgh; the month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: He acquires the rights to Misterogers and brings the material back to Fifth Avenue, where it is rebuilt for American public television as Mister Rogers' Neighborhood. Everything he has done in separate rooms now arrives in one place: the composition degree, the divinity degree, McFarland's child development, nine years of puppetry behind a set, and four years of standing in front of a camera in a country that was not his own. He is thirty-nine, and he has thirty-three years of the same half hour ahead of him.
suggested_refs: The 1967 transfer of rights in Misterogers from the CBC to Rogers

stops.name: WQED, the national premiere
stops.date_confidence: attested for the national premiere date and for the eventual total of 895 episodes
stops.campa: Mister Rogers' Neighborhood goes out nationally, distributed by National Educational Television from the Pittsburgh studio. The ritual is fixed from the first episode and will not change across 895 of them: the front door, the sweater off the hook, the street shoes swapped for sneakers, the trolley through the tunnel into the Neighborhood of Make-Believe, and the plain statement that the child watching is liked as he is. It is 1968, and the country outside the studio is coming apart.
stops.quote: You've made this day a special day, by just your being you. There's no person in the whole world like you, and I like you, just the way you are.
stops.quote_source: The programme's daily sign-off, quoted by Rogers in his testimony to the U.S. Senate Subcommittee on Communications, 1 May 1969, transcript via Speakola
suggested_refs: The premiere episode of Mister Rogers' Neighborhood, 19 February 1968

stops.name: The Russell Senate Office Building, six minutes before Pastore
stops.date_confidence: the date and the subcommittee are attested; the coordinate is the Russell Senate Office Building as a reasonable approximation for a 1969 Senate hearing, and no consulted source names the room
stops.campa: Twenty million dollars of federal funding for public broadcasting is on the table and about to be cut. Rogers takes the witness chair before Senator John Pastore, sets aside his prepared statement, and talks for six minutes about what a child can do with anger. He recites the words of a song instead of singing them. Pastore, who has been brusque with every witness before him, says he is moved and that the money is as good as approved. An entire broadcasting system survives on that exchange.
stops.quote: What do you do with the mad that you feel?
stops.quote_source: Rogers reciting the opening line of his song to Senator John Pastore, U.S. Senate Subcommittee on Communications, 1 May 1969, transcript via Speakola; Rogers adds in the same breath that the line came straight from a child
suggested_refs: Film of the 1 May 1969 testimony before Senator John Pastore's subcommittee
sources: Speakola and Current, 1969 Senate testimony transcript

stops.name: Latrobe, the father's death and the end of meat
stops.date_confidence: the year of the father's death and the turn to pescetarianism is attested; the month and day are placeholders, the coordinate is Latrobe at large, and the later turn to vegetarianism is dated by the source only to the early 1980s, the pool's specific 1982 being unsupported
stops.campa: James Hillis Rogers dies, and his son stops eating meat. He becomes pescetarian in the year of the funeral and gives up fish as well in the early 1980s. The brick company president whose business made the family prosperous is buried near Latrobe. The son goes back to Pittsburgh and to a programme that has been on the air two years and will run another thirty-one, and the eating rule holds for the rest of his life without being discussed on camera.
suggested_refs: The grave of James Hillis Rogers near Latrobe, Westmoreland County

stops.name: Washington, chair of the White House Conference on Children and Youth
stops.date_confidence: the appointment as chair in 1970 is attested; the month is a placeholder and no venue is given in any consulted source, so the coordinate is the White House as a Washington placeholder
stops.campa: He is appointed chair of the White House Conference on Children and Youth, which puts the man in the cardigan at the head of a federal body. His declared expertise is the interior weather of a five-year-old, and he is asked to speak for it in the register Washington runs on, which is the register of committees, findings, and appropriations. He has already proved, in a Senate hearing room nineteen months earlier, that this register can be broken open by a man who declines to raise his voice.
stops.quote: I give an expression of care every day to each child, to help him realize that he is unique.
stops.quote_source: U.S. Senate Subcommittee on Communications testimony, 1 May 1969, transcript via Speakola and Current
suggested_refs: The 1970 White House Conference on Children and Youth report

stops.name: Pittsburgh, Family Communications, Inc.
stops.date_confidence: the founding year of the nonprofit production company is attested; the month and day are placeholders and the coordinate is the WQED pin, no separate company address being given
stops.campa: He forms a nonprofit production company, Family Communications, Inc., to make his own programming, which means the Neighborhood belongs to no network and to no advertiser. There are no commercials in it and there never will be. A man who left NBC at twenty-five now owns the thing he makes, and the corporate structure is part of the argument rather than a wrapper around it: nothing is sold to the child, and the child is not sold on to anyone else either.
suggested_refs: The 1971 incorporation papers of Family Communications, Inc., Pittsburgh

stops.name: WQED, production stops
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1975 for the end of new production, with reruns continuing; the month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: He stops making new episodes. The programme does not leave the air, because the reruns continue and a preschool audience turns over completely every three years, so the country barely registers the pause. He is forty-seven. He has made the same half hour several hundred times, and he goes looking for something else to do with a television camera. What he finds is adults, and adults turn out to be the harder assignment. He will be back in this studio within four years.
suggested_refs: WQED production records for the 1975 suspension of new episodes

segments.name: The Second Half: Adults, Silence, Retirement

stops.name: Pittsburgh, Old Friends ... New Friends
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1978 for the thirty-minute adult interview programme and its run of twenty episodes; the month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: He hosts a thirty-minute interview programme for adults, Old Friends ... New Friends, and it runs for twenty episodes. The method is exactly the one he uses with children, which is to ask a question and then wait, and on adult television the waiting reads as a fault in the tape. Twenty episodes is not a failure and it is not a second career either. He puts the sweater back on and goes back to the audience that does not mind a silence. He is fifty years old.
suggested_refs: The twenty episodes of Old Friends ... New Friends, 1978

stops.name: WQED, production resumes
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1979 for the resumption, after a hiatus of roughly four years, 1975 to 1978; the pool's phrase five-year hiatus is bad arithmetic and is corrected. The month is a placeholder. The Sony testimony quoted here is dated by year only, the pool's 1979-09 being unverifiable
stops.campa: After roughly four years of reruns he begins making new episodes again, and he will keep making them for twenty-two more years. In the same year, under oath in a Los Angeles courtroom, he testifies for the defence in the case over home video recording, arguing that a parent who tapes his programme to watch later with a child is doing a good thing. Five years afterwards the Supreme Court of the United States will quote him in a footnote of the Betamax opinion.
stops.quote: You are an important person just the way you are. You can make healthy decisions.
stops.quote_source: Rogers' trial testimony in Universal City Studios v. Sony Corp. (C.D. Cal. 1979), quoted verbatim in Sony Corp. of America v. Universal City Studios, 464 U.S. 417, 446 n.27 (1984), citing trial record 2920-2921
suggested_refs: The Betamax opinion, 464 U.S. 417, footnote 27, quoting Rogers' testimony

stops.name: Radio City Music Hall, ten seconds
stops.date_confidence: attested: Wikipedia's 24th Daytime Emmy Awards gives 21 May 1997 at Radio City Music Hall and names Rogers as the Lifetime Achievement recipient, confirmed by American Rhetoric. Speakola labels the same transcript 14 September 1997 at the Pasadena Civic Auditorium, which is the 49th Primetime Emmys; that citation is rejected. The coordinate is coarse but lands on the building
stops.campa: The Daytime Emmys give him a Lifetime Achievement Award in a hall full of television people. He comes to the microphone and asks the room for ten seconds of silence to think of the people who loved them into being. The room, which is not built for stillness, holds it. He spends his own award making an audience of professionals sit quietly and think about somebody else, which is the same manoeuvre he has been running on four-year-olds every weekday since 1968.
stops.quote: So many people have helped me to come to this night. Some of you are here, some are far away, some are even in Heaven. All of us have special ones who have loved us into being. Would you just take, along with me, ten seconds to think of the people who have helped you become who you are.
stops.quote_source: Lifetime Achievement acceptance speech, 24th Annual Daytime Emmy Awards, Radio City Music Hall, New York, 21 May 1997, transcripts via Speakola and American Rhetoric
suggested_refs: Broadcast footage of the 24th Daytime Emmy Awards Lifetime Achievement presentation
sources: American Rhetoric, Fred Rogers Lifetime Achievement Emmy Award

stops.name: WQED, the last taping
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 2000 for the taping of the final episode; the day is not given and is defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The final episode is taped on Fifth Avenue. Thirty-three years of the same set, the same door, the same trolley running on the same few feet of track through the same tunnel, and then the tape stops. He is seventy-two. The studio lights go up on a man taking off a cardigan for the last time on camera, and the tape sits in a Pittsburgh vault for nine months before the country is allowed to see it. The set is struck and the props go into boxes that will end up in an archive outside Latrobe.
suggested_refs: The final taping at WQED, December 2000

stops.name: WQED, the last broadcast
stops.date_confidence: attested for the airing of the final original episode and for his retirement at age seventy-three
stops.campa: The last original episode airs and the national run of Mister Rogers' Neighborhood ends after thirty-three years and 895 episodes. He retires at seventy-three. The reruns keep going, as they did through the 1970s, so for most of the audience nothing perceptible happens on this day at all. The man who came home from Toronto in 1967 with a box of rights has spent every working year since inside one building on one street in one city. On the last day the door opens the way it opened on the first.
stops.quote: Whomever you've been thinking about, how pleased they must be to know the difference you feel they've made.
stops.quote_source: Lifetime Achievement acceptance speech, 24th Annual Daytime Emmy Awards, 21 May 1997, transcripts via Speakola and American Rhetoric
suggested_refs: The final broadcast episode of Mister Rogers' Neighborhood, 31 August 2001

stops.name: Dartmouth College, the last commencement address
stops.date_confidence: the address is attested to 2002 by Wikipedia and dated 9 June 2002 by the SingjuPost transcript; the coordinate repeats the Dartmouth Green pin used for his year of study in 1946
stops.campa: He returns to the Green he left after a single year in 1947 and gives the last commencement address of his life. He tells the graduating class that what is essential is invisible to the eye, in French first and then in English, and he quotes the cellist Yo-Yo Ma on the sound that no one else can make. Then he asks for a full unbroken minute of silence to remember those who loved them into being, and he holds several thousand people to it. He has eight months to live.
stops.quote: L'essentiel est invisible pour les yeux. What is essential is invisible to the eye.
stops.quote_source: Dartmouth College commencement address, 9 June 2002, Rogers quoting Antoine de Saint-Exupery's The Little Prince in French and then in English, transcript via SingjuPost
suggested_refs: The Dartmouth commencement address of 9 June 2002, full transcript

stops.name: The East Room of the White House, the Medal of Freedom
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date, the President, and the East Room
stops.campa: George W. Bush hangs the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest civilian honour the country gives, around the neck of a children's television host. Four weeks earlier, on the Dartmouth Green, the same man told a graduating class what actually feeds a soul, and it was not this. He is seventy-four. The citation covers a body of work made entirely of half hours in which almost nothing happens: a man comes in, changes his shoes, speaks slowly to one person, and says the same thing a hundred ways.
stops.quote: It's not the honors and the prizes and the fancy outsides of life which ultimately nourish our souls.
stops.quote_source: Dartmouth College commencement address, 9 June 2002, one month before the Medal of Freedom, transcript via SingjuPost
suggested_refs: Photographs of the 9 July 2002 Presidential Medal of Freedom ceremony in the East Room

stops.name: Pittsburgh, the diagnosis and the surgery
stops.date_confidence: the diagnosis is attested to October 2002 and the stomach surgery to 6 January 2003; the day of the diagnosis is not given and is defaulted to 01, the coordinate is the Squirrel Hill neighbourhood centroid and no hospital is named. The pool's afterlife lens said he was diagnosed only weeks before his death, which contradicts its own chronology and is rejected
stops.campa: A stomach cancer is found in October. He has surgery on the sixth of January and it does not save him. The illness is kept largely private, which is consistent enough: for thirty-three years he told children that feelings are mentionable and manageable, and about his own body he told the public almost nothing. Between the diagnosis and the death there are four months, and no episode, no statement, and no farewell broadcast is made in them. He is seventy-four.
suggested_refs: Contemporary Pittsburgh press coverage of Rogers' January 2003 surgery

stops.name: Squirrel Hill, the death
stops.date_confidence: the date, the age of seventy-four, his wife's presence and the last rites are attested. Wikipedia says only his Pittsburgh home, so the coordinate is the Squirrel Hill centroid rather than an address. The pool's geography lens called this one month after his seventy-fifth birthday, which is backwards: born 20 March 1928, he dies three weeks before it
stops.campa: He dies at his Pittsburgh home, aged seventy-four, three weeks short of his seventy-fifth birthday. Joanne is with him. Archabbot Douglas Nowicki of Saint Vincent, the Latrobe archabbey beside the college that will hold his archive, has given him the last rites. A Presbyterian minister ordained to television receives the last rites of a Benedictine, in a house on a hill above the city where every one of his 895 episodes was made. He had been ordained forty years.
suggested_refs: The Rogers residence in Squirrel Hill, Pittsburgh, address unrecorded in consulted sources

stops.name: Unity Chapel, the private funeral and the McFeely mausoleum
stops.date_confidence: the private funeral at Unity Chapel on 1 March 2003 and the interment in a mausoleum owned by his mother's family are attested. Three coordinates for this cemetery circulate in the pool, 40.2953 / -79.3567 and 40.3115 / -79.3765 and the Nominatim geocode used here; the first is about 5.5 km out in open country and the second about 3.6 km east
stops.campa: The funeral is private, held at Unity Chapel in Unity Cemetery outside Latrobe, and he is laid in a mausoleum owned by his mother's family, the McFeelys, whose name was on the brick company and is his own middle name. He is buried thirty-five miles from Pittsburgh and a few miles from the house where he was born. That is the entire geography of the life, closed: two Pennsylvania towns, and a working life spent going back and forth between the two of them.

stops.name: Heinz Hall, the public memorial
stops.date_confidence: the date and the figure of about 2,700 attending are attested; the coordinate is the Nominatim geocode of Heinz Hall, replacing the pool's 40.4407 / -79.9958, about 550 m southeast
stops.campa: About 2,700 people fill Heinz Hall in downtown Pittsburgh for the public service. Itzhak Perlman plays, Yo-Yo Ma appears by video, and the organist Alan Morrison plays the hall's instrument. The city that got him back from Toronto in 1967 says goodbye to him in a concert hall rather than a church, which for a minister ordained to a camera is the correct room. He had told Tom Junod, five years before, what he thought heaven probably was. Two thousand seven hundred people, and no sermon.
stops.quote: The connections we make in the course of a life, maybe that's what heaven is, Tom.
stops.quote_source: Tom Junod, 'Can You Say...Hero?', Esquire, November 1998, Rogers speaking to Junod; a comma is substituted for the source's dash per house style and the wording is otherwise unaltered

stops.name: Saint Vincent College, Latrobe, the centre in his name
stops.date_confidence: the centre, now the Fred Rogers Institute, is attested by Wikipedia's Saint Vincent College article, which upgrades the pool's tentative tag; the founding year 2003 is plausible but not independently confirmed, and the coordinate is Wikipedia's figure for the college, replacing two different and both wrong pairs in the pool, 40.3402 / -79.4033 and 40.3193 / -79.3903. The claim that Rogers was a college trustee is unsourced and dropped
stops.campa: A centre for early learning and children's media is established in his name at Saint Vincent College outside Latrobe, on the campus of the Benedictine archabbey whose archabbot gave him the last rites. He was working on it before he died. It becomes the Fred Rogers Institute and holds the archive: scripts, correspondence, sweaters, puppets, more than twenty thousand items belonging to a life that produced almost nothing except television. The Benedictines keep the papers of a Presbyterian.

stops.name: WQED, the studio takes his name
stops.date_confidence: the renaming is attested but dated in the source only to after 2003, so the month and day here are declared placeholders; the name and address are independently confirmed by the 2018 USPS release
stops.campa: The station renames its production studio the Fred Rogers Studio. It is the room he came to in 1953 when the place had a licence and no programmes, the room he left for Toronto and came back to, and the room where all 895 episodes were shot. The address, 4802 Fifth Avenue, will be printed on a United States Postal Service national release fifteen years later as though it were a landmark of the republic, which by then it is. The name goes over the door of a room whose entire content was a man taking off a jacket and putting on a sweater.
suggested_refs: The Fred Rogers Studio at WQED, 4802 Fifth Avenue, Pittsburgh

stops.name: North Shore Riverfront Park, Tribute to Children
stops.date_confidence: the sculptor Robert Berks and the Pittsburgh Fred Rogers Memorial are attested by Wikipedia, which lists the work as 2009 and says he completed it in 2007. The specific unveiling date of 5 November 2009 could not be corroborated, the cited Post-Gazette page returning 404, and an Overpass query returns no feature for the statue, so the coordinate is unverified
stops.campa: Robert Berks, who made the Einstein that sits at the National Academy of Sciences in Washington, sets a bronze Rogers on the Allegheny riverfront across from downtown: seated, leaning forward, tying a sneaker. It is the gesture the programme opened with for thirty-three years, cast at monument scale beside the football stadium. Pittsburgh walkers call it the Fred Rogers statue and do not use the title on the plaque, which reads Tribute to Children.

stops.name: Latrobe, the state historical marker
stops.date_confidence: the dedication date is attested; no consulted source gives the marker's location, so the coordinate is Latrobe at large
stops.campa: Pennsylvania bolts up a cast metal historical marker in Latrobe, the kind that stands at battlefields, furnaces, and inventors' workshops, and the text on this one is about a man who talked to preschool children. Eighty-eight years after the birth on Main Street, the commonwealth files him among its generals and its industrialists. The town that called him Fat Freddy now carries his name at the roadside for drivers to read at twenty-five miles an hour.

stops.name: WQED, the Forever stamp
stops.date_confidence: attested directly from the primary source: the USPS national release pr18_018 gives first day of issue as Friday 23 March 2018 at 11 a.m. ET at WQED's Fred Rogers Studio, 4802 5th Avenue, Pittsburgh PA 15213. The release does not describe the stamp art, so the King Friday XIII detail rests on other sourcing
stops.campa: At eleven in the morning the Postal Service issues a Forever stamp in his honour, first day of issue at WQED's Fred Rogers Studio on Fifth Avenue. The image pairs him with King Friday XIII. A hand puppet built for a local Pittsburgh children's programme in 1954 is now on federal postage, and the man who worked that puppet from behind a set for nine years before anyone saw his face is standing beside it on the same square of paper. The stamp costs whatever a letter costs, forever.
stops.quote: The number 143 means 'I love you.' It takes one letter to say 'I' and four letters to say 'love' and three letters to say 'you.'
stops.quote_source: Tom Junod, 'Can You Say...Hero?', Esquire, November 1998, Rogers quoted directly

stops.name: Pittsburgh, the revival on film
stops.date_confidence: the release date of the documentary is attested; the box-office superlative is relayed from Focus Features data and 2018 trade reporting that was not audited in this pass, and neither film carries a place in the pool, so the coordinate is downtown Pittsburgh as a declared placeholder
stops.campa: Morgan Neville's documentary Won't You Be My Neighbor? opens and becomes one of the highest-grossing biographical documentaries in American box-office history, and the press names what follows a Fred Rogers revival. The next year Tom Hanks plays him in a feature adapted from Tom Junod's Esquire profile. A country seventeen years past the last new episode goes looking for the man in the cardigan, and the footage it finds has not aged, nor has the argument running underneath it.
